articleTitle: On-line current monitoring to detect electrical and mechanical faults in three-phase induction motor drives
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: To prevent the sudden failure of a large motor which can be very costly and potentially dangerous, it is essential that fault mechanisms are detected at an early stage while the machine is still in service. It is therefore beneficial to have an on-line monitoring system to detect incipient trouble and thus enable planned preventive maintenance or repair to be carried out. Here, the author presents study results which show that online spectrum analysis of motor current can be used to detect broken rotor bars, dynamic eccentricity and purely mechanical malfunctions such as rotor misalignment or a worn pump in induction motor drive systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of a data historian to extend plant life
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Power stations have always spent much effort collecting data about plant. operation. Since much of this data is paper based, it cannot easily be converted into information to help people do their jobs better. Power plants using more than a few percent of their history of production in decision processes are rare. The purpose of this paper is to describe some specific historian software, the Plant Information System, which is used to collect, compress, store, validate and present real time and historical data. The approach to data recording and storage is described as well as the problems of interfacing with the data sensor systems in the plant and the collection of this data. The influence of the dramatic advances in the power and functionality of desktop computing resources is considered, and finally some examples are given of how historian software may be used in the life management of power plants.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Non-invasive instrumentation for on-line management and monitoring of electrical plant
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Accurate and reliable instrumentation is obviously necessary for the cost effective and efficient operation and management of modern electromechanical power plant. Machine parameters such as current, speed and torque are routinely monitored via dedicated transducers and provide the basis for routine plant operational control and maintenance strategies. The work reported in this paper reflects the opinion that machine and plant monitoring should develop as a holistic process whereby a variety of machine parameters and techniques are used not only to monitor day to day operational requirements but also to provide information and diagnoses on the long term health of plant.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planned maintenance of high voltage rotating machine insulation based upon information derived from on-line discharge measurements
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The drive to obtain improvements in plant economy, availability and useful operating life has led to an increasing interest in the possibility of monitoring all aspects of machine condition whilst the plant is operating in normal service. On-line monitoring of discharge activity in the stator winding structure can give a sensitive indication of degradation processes so long as individual discharge events are detected and measured. The discharge characteristic so obtained is that which the machine exhibits continuously in normal service and is influenced by service conditions such as physical movement which cannot be simulated in an off-line test. Regular monitoring provides the opportunity for early detection of problems and possible remedial action to prolong winding life, or for scheduling of rewind operations during routine shutdown periods. This paper describes an on-line discharge monitoring system which has been extensively applied to machines in service and presents case studies to illustrate the correlation between measured discharge characteristics and winding condition.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Theoretical base for on-line control of cable electric lines
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The author presents a theoretical method for the online disconnection (nonoperation) of a cable electric line (CEL). The method consists in measuring/controlling the conduction current through the insulation system of a CEL. The fundamentals of this concept require certain conditions and can be applied only to CELs which are yet to be manufactured-i.e. new lines and those having an extruded protection sheath.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On-line monitoring of rotor shorted turns
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Large generators for use with steam and gas turbines are subject to high mechanical and electrical stress which may lead to deterioration of the insulation. The rotors, in particular, may develop short circuits and there is a need for the operators to be aware of this situation. The manner in which shorted turns can occur in the rotors of generators and the difficulties associated with monitoring for such shorted turns are indicated. An online monitor which has been developed to solve this problem is described together with some operating experiences which have been learnt from the use of it.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: In service inspection of Calder Hall and Chapelcross nuclear power stations
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: In the context of continued operation, BNF plc. carry out inspections of operational plant as a means of supporting the safety case. Economic viability is an essential part of the case for continued operation and has resulted in the development of a number of cost-effective techniques for nuclear power plant inspection. This paper briefly outlines two such techniques: ultrasonic inspection of the Calder Hall and Chapelcross reactor pressure vessels; and visual inspection of core support brackets.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Assessing the effect of thermal transients on the life of boiler plant
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Currently difficulties exist for the design engineer confronted with the design or assessment of conventional steam power plant boiler components which operate in a creep-fatigue environment. These arise from the ultra-conservative methods available and the paucity of data describing the creep-fatigue interaction mechanism. The author describes how Babcock have utilised a hybrid method to analyse the creep-fatigue life of boiler components. The method is believed to provide sufficient conservatism while still maintaining economically designed components. Use of the finite element method for thermal and stress analysis aids in the correlation between operational events and damage mechanisms. A novel method of online monitoring of thermal fatigue has been developed based on finite element analysis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Predictive modelling of long term creep performance of critical plant components
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: In their common form, continuum damage models describe only the secondary and tertiary stages of creep. Various methods have been used to incorporate primary creep; these are noted in this paper and their implications for life and ductility prediction discussed. For component remanent life prediction, a simple method, involving a single additional materials parameter, is recommended. The application of the method is illustrated and the implications for materials data collection and analysis are considered. The approach is demonstrated on low alloy steels.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A manufacturers contribution to life management of transformers
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Power transformers have a long expectation of life, but transformers do eventually fail. It is important to appreciate that if the average life of a family of transformers is 40 years, half of that family will have failed within 40 years. Whereas many transmission transformers are operated at only half load for much of their life, generator transformers in power stations usually operate at or near full load for more than 80% of their lives. The determination of the remnant life of transformers is a goal pursued by many researchers, but it is unlikely to be achieved in the near future. However, it is possible to determine the probable condition of transformers, and this information can provide useful guidance in the life management of transformers. In the past the majority of life management decisions have been made by the purchaser, but the manufacturer has an important part to play and judgements made based on inputs from both parties will be more informed. A new understanding between manufacturer and purchaser would provide a synergy to improve commercial inter-relationship.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Prediction of nitric oxide formation in new furnace designs using the results from computational fluid dynamics
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: A method has been described which can predict the rate of formation of nitric oxide in a power generating combustor using the velocity and temperature results obtained from combustion flows. The results have been compared with experimental measurements and it has been found that the temperatures used are crucial in predicting nitric oxide concentration. The method could be applied to new furnace designs to reduce thermal NO/sub x/ production.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cumulative life assessment system for the Hunterston B reactors
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The Hunterston B nuclear power station, operated by Scottish Nuclear Limited, incorporates two advanced gas cooled reactors (AGR), with a total capacity of 1150 MW. These units have operated very successfully since they were commissioned in 1976, with a planned load factor close to 80% by the end of 1994. This paper describes a cumulative life assessment system software package (CLASS) which is designed to perform life usage calculations for specified Hunterston AGR components using actual reactor histories and existing analyses.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Surface replication of power plant components
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The large visual inspection and nondestructive testing programmes carried out as part of major power plant overhauls normally identify many features which require to be accurately recorded or further examined to determine their nature and severity. In many cases, due to the shape of the components concerned and/or access, direct visual and microscopic examination may not be possible and indirect examination of a replica made of the feature or area concerned may be the preferred method of examination. The author describes how, in response to this requirement within the power generation industry, three main replication methods have been developed: bulk replication; macro replication; and micro replication.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Revitalisation of distribution network
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The island of Bahrain is served via over 3200 ground-mounted 11 kV/415 V distribution substations (comprising a ring main unit, a transformer, and a low voltage panel) and over 750 pole mounted transformers with much of the network underground. Such severe operating conditions are taking their toll on the distribution plant. Much of the equipment in use were not designed to operate at such ambient temperatures and hence, measures had to be taken towards derating some of the equipment in use. Here, the authors present an outline of the revitalisation project for the Bahrain distribution network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Predictive stress and crack growth monitoring in cracked superheater headers
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: This paper summarises the component life assessment strategy used by PowerGen to underwrite the continued operation of high capital cost components which contain defects, such as ligament cracking in boiler steam headers. The life assessment strategy consists of three separate stages, where at each stage more effort is expended and subsequently better, and generally longer, component life estimates are made. Benefits from this process are that the impact of changes in modes of operation, such as entering a two-shift mode of operation can be relatively easily assessed, and that cracked components can often be shown to be safe to remain in service, in some cases for many years.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The ultrasonic inspection of rotors from the bore using an automated ultrasonic inspection system
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Comprehensive life extension services have been developed by turbine generator manufacturers, including Parsons, to assure the integrity and maximise the safe life of turbine plant. The life assessment comprises a thorough nondestructive and metallurgical examination of critical components in conjunction with a stress analysis using lower bound material properties. In addition a complete rehabilitation and retro-fitting service is also offered for the repair and upgrading of turbine plant. The ultrasonic inspection of rotors from the bore by PRIES (Parsons Rotor Inspection and Evaluation System), a fully automatic computer controlled inspection system, is one part of this service. The EPRI NDE Centre has completed an independent evaluation of test data collected by the system on bore blocks containing artificial and natural defects. Results show the detection rates to be among the highest achievable, together with a high degree of positional and sizing accuracy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Condition monitoring and predictive analysis of combined heat and power systems
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The use of small-scale power generating equipment covers a number of configurations adapted for use across an extensive range of applications. The content of this paper considers an approach to condition monitoring and predictive maintenance applied to standby diesel generators and small-scale combined heat and power (CHP) systems. The system described was originally designed to meet the monitoring and control requirements for standby diesel generators, but its potential was quickly realised and the system has now been developed for use in CHP applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Risk based inspection-developments in the USA
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: In 1985, under the direction of the Council of Engineering, the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) formed a Risk Analysis Task Force to consider the use of risk based methods In the formulation of policies, codes and standards. In 1988, following the recommendations of this Task Force, the ASME Centre for Research established a research programme to determine how risk-based methods could be used to establish inspection requirements. Here, the author presents an overview of the current development status of risk-based inspection in the USA.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Overview of EDF's approach
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The authors discuss the life management of Electricite de France's nuclear and fossil fired power stations. For the fossil fired units the authors discuss environmental criteria for coal units, oil units and combustion turbines. The authors then discuss the safety and economical aspects of PWR units.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated plant automation, control and monitoring systems: a new heart for an old station
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Technological advances have enabled the control and monitoring processes required at power stations to be fully integrated. This integration permits productivity improvements to be gained through more efficient management of the overall production process. This paper discusses the retrofitting of fully integrated control and monitoring systems at Swanbank, the Queensland Electricity Commission's oldest operating thermal power station situated in the heart of the main load centre of South East Queensland. Swanbank power station has 6*68 MW and 4*125 MW turbogenerator units, all of which have been recommissioned with the new control systems and are now fully operational.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The refurbishment of Sloy power station (hydroelectric power)
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Loch Sloy was the first hydroelectric power scheme developed by Scottish Hydro Electric's predecessor, the North of Scotland Hydro Electric Board. It was built primarily to supply electrical power to Clydeside and Central Scotland and was officially opened by the Queen Mother in 1950. In recent years, the plant at Sloy has exhibited signs of serious deterioration of the mechanical integrity of runners and electrical integrity of generator winding insulation. The authors describe how, in order to secure its asset, Scottish Hydro Electric initiated a programme to refurbish Sloy power station over a five year period concluding in 1996.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MHD repowering for environmental control and capacity addition
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) is one of number of advanced power generating technologies being investigated by many world laboratories. This technology, upon successful development, will result in a direct coal burning power generation system having significantly higher efficiency, lower environmental intrusion, and lower generation costs than existing conventional electrical generation plant. The authors address the question as to whether the most economical way to clean up the stack would be to repower the plant with an MHD topping cycle. This approach also provides additional capacity by the amount of net power generated by the MHD topping cycle. Since additional capacity is needed in Poland and the USA, this appears to be an attractive feature. In this paper, the authors have developed the conceptual design, calculate the performance, and estimate the capital costs for repowering a Polish power plant with MHD.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Valve developments in reducing the costs of power generation
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The economics of purchasing and operating power plants depends on the relative costs of capital equipment, fuel, labour, etc, all of which can change with time. Thus, after an interval of time, it is possible to re-examine the costings of power generation and to possibly identify improvements. Here, the author describes how valves have a useful role to play in minimising the operating costs of power plants, and examples of two main areas of interest are examined: (1) reducing direct costs by improving plant efficiency, lowering flow losses, reducing fluid leaks, etc; and (2) minimising the indirect costs of maintenance, repair and replacement.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Condition assessment technologies for power plant boiler refractories
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Refractory linings are used to provide protection against erosion, corrosion and high temperatures. The water wall tubes near the burners in conventional fossil plant (especially fired by low volatile coal) may be coated by a thin layer of refractory applied by brushing or spraying. This paper reviews existing and future technologies which could potentially be used for the condition assessment of power plant refractories. It is based on an extensive survey carried out by ERA Technology and CERAM Research in support of a proposed multi-client research programme to develop new condition assessment technologies for refractory asset management and is known as the CATRAM project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Structural integrity assessments of power plant components: the R5 and R6 procedures
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Failures of power generating plant have serious economic and safety implications. The availability of validated assessment methods enables routine structural integrity assessments to be performed as aids to: (i) safety case acceptance; (ii) planning of outages and repair and inspection strategies; and (iii) plant life extension arguments. The requirement to regularly perform such assessments within Nuclear Electric and the former Central Electricity Generating Board (CEGB) has led to the development of the assessment procedures R5 and R6. These procedures are described and recent advances highlighted. An example of the use of R5 to analyse the failure of a welded steel pressure vessel is given. The conservatism of the assessment procedure is emphasised.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience and improvement of power plant operation due to continuous monitoring of boiler drum life
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: This paper deals with the operating experience of the power plant life extension. The scope is the range of thick wall vessels operating at temperatures below 400 degrees C. Boiler drums with the same material properties have suffered ruptures during pressure test after repairs. The main concern was focused on the high life use during the ambient temperature 1.5 p pressure test. With growing experience the evaluation of fatigue is extended to normal operation start up and shut off periods. Some components within the power plant proved, based on analyses from the DMS, not to be fit for the required performance. The systems have been enhanced and have successfully reduced the fatigue sources.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Welding solutions for turbine generator plant repair, upgrade and life extension
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: New opportunities are being presented to power generation plant operators and manufacturers with the development of methods for the repair and refurbishment of turbines and ancillary plant. The philosophy and experiences of Parsons Power Generation Systems Limited are presented to demonstrate the important role that welding plays in the provision of cost-effective solutions for ensuring power plant availability, improvement of operational integrity and life extension.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Intelligent power plant control, for enhanced life management
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The important issues associated with maximising the use of capital assets, limiting down time, extending life and minimising operational and support cost of power stations, are key areas which warrant continuous attention. Today online, high performance intelligent systems with complementary IT tools, can provide improved plant protection, operational and support and therefore enhanced plant life management. The paper shows how the application and integration of intelligent systems with current technology can most effectively and economically deliver improved power plant protection through significantly improving the application of important maintenance and support routines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Planned lifetime management increasing availability and reducing costs
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The author suggests that support and maintenance of operating plants is a necessary evil. We can't do without it, but we would prefer to if we could! This paper explains the process being used by Rolls Royce and Associates (RRA) to help reduce this support burden and improve the effectiveness of complex plants. The author introduces RRA, outlines the maintenance problem, then explains the approach with some practical examples.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Plant lifetime management-an integrated approach
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Rapid change in the power generation industry requires a re-appraisal of the roles of the power producers and their main contractors. The contractors must recognise the competitive pressure on clients, and mobilise their total capability to achieve a profitable return from the capital assets employed during a time of unprecedented change. The generators have available to them, through their contractors, considerable potential to extend the economic life of existing plant. Forging new relationships to utilise this potential is a challenge to both power producer and contractor alike.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Commissioning of static excitation on a 600 MW cross compound generator
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: NEI Control Systems have been supplying excitation control systems for use on turbogenerator plant for 25 years. The early systems were based on analogue controllers combined with a three phase thyristor bridge to supply the exciter or generator field current. In response to customer requirements these systems were refined over the years to: (i) provide more features in the controller; (ii) provide larger outputs from the thyristor converter; and (iii) to achieve higher availability by means of redundancy in both the controller and the convertor. The very latest designs are based on digital techniques many of which have been developed from the Company's established range of electro-hydraulic governors. The first part of the paper reviews some of the possible redundancy architectures and outlines how the most appropriate redundancy techniques have been chosen and applied to the various parts of the excitation system. The second part describes in detail the testing procedures and the tuning requirement to satisfy grid system objectives.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Plant life extension for Torness nuclear power station
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Torness nuclear power station comprises two advanced gas-cooled reactors (AGR) each with an original design rating of 16OOMW(Th). The first unit was commissioned in May 1988 and the second unit in February of the following year. This paper describes the systematic approach adopted in developing the case for life extension at Torness. The incentives for power plant life extension are discussed as are the dominant life limiting processes. The results of the study are for the in-reactor metallic components and for the graphite moderator.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Economic considerations underlying the adoption of reliability-centred maintenance
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Despite suggestions which claim substantial benefits can be realized by embracing reliability-centred maintenance (RCM), serious difficulties have been encountered during its application. In many industries, including electricity transmission, implementation is forestalled by an inability to obtain quantitative results from the pilot study phase. This inability can, in part, be attributed to a general failure by would-be practitioners to suitably address the fundamental argument surrounding the introduction; whether RCM will, or will not, prove economically beneficial. To ensure profitable RCM applications, a rigorous financial evaluation must serve as a prelude to implementation; by regarding its introduction as an investment decision, by identifying, and subsequently quantifying, the true benefits of RCM, more successful applications can ensue. Such an evaluation framework, developed by the National Grid Company ple (NGC) and the University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology (UMIST), designed to address the shortcomings of traditional methods of RCM appraisal, is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A probabilistic approach to assessing AGR core life
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: The authors provide an overview of the early stages of a new approach for assessing the integrity of AGR graphite cores which incorporates improved methods and accommodates the presence of broken reactor components using a probabilistic treatment. Nuclear Electric has been developing this methodology based upon the probabilistic analysis of core ageing and component failure with a computer code CORSET. The code examines the distortion of the core under various operating conditions, allowing for local discontinuities due to component failure. These distortions are repeatedly assessed allowing for statistical variations in component dimensions and properties, thus constructing a probabilistic distribution against which the required operational and safety features can be confirmed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Hunterston 'B' advanced gas cooled reactor-development of electrical auxiliary system with station life
publicationTitle: International Conference on Life Management of Power Plants 1994
abstract: Construction of Hunterston B nuclear power station started in the late 1960s and the station commenced operation in 1976. The nuclear plant comprises two advanced gas-cooled reactors (AGR) providing steam at high pressure and temperature to two dedicated 660 MW steam turbine generators. From the time of commissioning, the operating history has been one of steady improvement in load factor, which was further enhanced by the start of on-load refuelling operations in 1983. This improvement has been achieved by the development and refinement of operation and maintenance procedures and by a steady process of modification to improve the performance and reliability of the reactor and conventional plant. These developments have necessarily involved the auxiliary power systems and equipment and the purpose of this paper is to describe the most significant of the changes made in this area of the power plant.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
